TERRIBLE TORNiDO IN AMERICA. GREAT LOSS OF LIPE. TRAINS WRECKED.-IWILDINGS DESTROYED. A TOWN ENVELOPED IN FLAMES.

None Toms, Tuttn.sPsv Moitnxtt.—Details of the fear- ful devastation wrought Inv the formai, wink!, visited" the Eastern States yestericav are hoorly arriving here; and frisn these it is easily Seen that the hurricane rin.t have been of great fierceness and magnitude. It swept eastwards through Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and New York States. The chief damage was done in the town of Pittsburg, Reading, and Williamsport, scores of buildings were wrecked, property sinashel and hundreds of persons either killed inr severely injur.l. In tine town of Mailing, Pennsylvania, where the tornado was very severe, Messrs. Cirimeshaw's silk mill was completely demolished. All the employes, amounting to over 200, were at work int the time, and all were injured, many fatally. It was , piteous to see the poor wretches struggling in the dilnis i with shattered limbs and agonisenl features imploring for help. ThOSOWhO went only slightly injured gave valu- able aid to their wounded comrades. The railioad in the vicinity was completely torn up, and several trains were wrecked during the first fierce blast of the hurricane, anil in Reading, itself nearly all the shops and large buildings were rased to the ground. Great excitement and terror were added to the scene by the outlestak of fire in several houses, and it looked at one time as if the mist to town would be enveloped in the flames, an quickly did tine fierce wind drive the sparks in every direction. All telegraphic communication has been cut off from the I town, and no further details have yet come to hand. It is known that several sliopmen were killed, and many injured. Besides this utter collapse of the Germania Bank-buildings, and several adjoining houses, many mills, dwelling-houses, andshops in Pittsburg have bon ruined. The hurricane here raged wills great furs- for over ten minutes. tin the town of Williamsport, Min-ea dozen houses and factories were wrecked, and nanny per- ton killed and injured. The ',mall of Sunbury, ' Penns., Wtao also visited severely, a nail mill there being blown down, and two persons killed and ten injured severely. The large Industrial tidal, tine City Armoury, and other buildings in Carlisle, Penns., fell to tine I ground with a great mash When the school ings collapuel the estholars were all at work, and ' few of them escaped without receiving injuries more or t less severe. Many persons were killed aud maimed he life in the town, and many still remain under the fallen Webers. Passengers of trains which escaped being I wrecked report that in the smaller towns in the Eastern t States the tornado raged with the same fury, and a corresponding loss of life and property must be inferred. It is stated that in Pittsburg, which seems to have I suffered the most, the scenes accompanying the disaster were most lamentable. All business has been suspended In despair, and the work of extricating the dead and dying hail to be abandoned. As evening closed the cries :Mil groans of the poor victims asthey lay helpless le-neith the ruins were piteous in the extreme. A sad aerident happened to a rescue party during the afternoon. II bile they were endeavouring to extricate some persons under a wall it fell upon them, and almost the whole party whieh included a maned and several firemen, were severely injured, and some, it is (earns', will not survive ' the shock. A hurricane cleats, snow, and wind, theugh in a lesser degree than that which has visited the Fast, prevails all over the countly. Seventy deaths have resulted from the catastrophe at Reading, Pennsylvania, and twenty from the Pittsburg accident.

A WARRINGTON PUBLICAN'S INTRIGr E. At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, before Alderman Holmes and Harrison, a case was heard in which Thomas Massey (26), manager of the Rodney public-house. Winwick-et. Warrington. I was brought up under a warrant charged with bar- ing committed a breach of the peace by assaulting , his wife, Martha Massey, on the previous day. Ile pleaded not guilty. The circumstances of the case, as narrated by the Chief Constable, were singular. Massey, Mr. Hunt said, hail been in the employ of Messrs. Walker and Sons, brewers, between six and seven years. Ile had up to the present borne an unblemished character. He bad been married for something like six years, and had led a happy life until four or five months ago. Within the past month Croix weeks the wife had got an idea that her husband intended to go abroad. A number of letters had been addressed to a David Thomas in care of the defendant, and this made his wife sus- picious. On Monday morning she saw one of these letters and read the contents. She was in conse- quence' • led to believe that her husband had been keeping company with another woman in Liverpool, who signed her name as Elisabeth Turner, and dated , the letter from 59 (loodson-road. Walton, Liverpool. Mrs. Massey after reading the letter, went to Liver- pool and saw the writer of it, who told her that : defendant had styled himself a single man, and had ! been keeping company with her since last October. On Tuesday morning a quarrel took place between the complainant and her husband, and the former assert.' that defendant threw her down, and took from tier a purse containing money. Conipl4nant went to Ito, police station, and made a statement to the Chief Constable. A warrant was then issued, and a watch was kept for the defendant, who wan on Tuesday night tle•ell to rush into the Central Station, and enter the 9.50 train for Liverpool, without having taken a ticket. lie was taken out and brought to the police station. His intention appeared to have been to go to America with the woman at Liverpool whose acquaintance he had made.--Complainant aid on Tuesday her husband, after being out all night, came into the house, and , she naked him what he was going to do—if lie would make terms with her. Ile refuted to give her any answer, and afterwards declined to make any terms. She took a few things away and would not bring them back. in her telling ! him so, he knocked her down on the stairs. , She afterwards went into the kitchen, where he threw heron the sofa, and dimanded her puree.— The defendant made a stat.-meat to the Bench to the effect that some few months ago he was going from ' Liverpool to New Brighton, and on the heat he got into conversation with a woman belonging to Liverpool. lie remained in her company at New Brighton all the afternoon, and went back to Liver- pooi with her. Since then lot had ocessaionally corresponded with her. Ile had never told her that he was a married man, because she had never put the question straight to him. Ile entirely denied the assatilt.—Ablerman Harrison It was your duty to tell her that you were a married man.--Defendant I have told her before now. - Alderman Holmes : You have no right to be writing letters to a young lady, and leading her to believe that you are a single young man.- - Alderman Harrison: Your duty is to attend to your /rife, and you have no right to go flirting with other women.-- The Bench ordered the defendant to enter into his own recognisances of .C4O to keep the peace for six months, and to find two sureties in -eat each. The sureties were forth- coming—At the Borough Police Court yesterday morning, the license of the Rodney public-house was transferred fmm Massey to John Marsh, late of Walker's Vaults, Seotland-rotol, temporary autho- rity to sell at the latter place being granted to George Lunt.

THRILLINO EXPERIENCE OF A CUNARD B.S. COMPANY'S ENGINEER. A leading Liverpool daily paper says "A day or two ago a gentleman, while in conversation with a prominent army °nicer, was made acquaint oil with a most thrilling experience of one of the oldest engineers in Liverpool. The name of the latter gentleman is Mr. William Buchanan, who, upon being visited, made the following statement : "1 have been twenty-four years in the service of the Cunard Steamship Company ; I reside at 81 Derby-road, Kirkdale, Liverpool. Two pars ago, while attending church, I was soddenly attacked with a most excruciat- ing pain in my head, which completely prostrated me ; 1 had ti be conveyed to tin- home. Then followed twelve months of agony, which is utterly imponsible to describe. I had to resign iny position, being entirdv incapacitated Clean work. Medical opinion was divided as to what my malady really was. One doctor decided that 1 WIL9 suffering from a rheumatic affection of the brain, another that it was an overflow of 11100,1 to the brain and a third that it was acute neuralgia. All agreed. however, that it would lead to softening of the brain. Six of the moot eminent physicians in Liveriepol attendigi me, but affonlol no relief. My case was regard.' as incurable, and my suffer- ings we re re so gat that I often became unconscious and fairly entry from pain. I could neither see nor hear for days at a time, and during the fearful attacks of pain my cries often attracted the atten- tion of my neighbours. My how, was pointed out as one in which a limn may lay at death's door, and sow of my paroxysms of pain Were to great, that it re- quired two and sometimes three strong men to hold me in bed. My physicians held consultations, but all of no avail. My sufferings remained the nime. My family were in despair, sari at onetime they regarded me so near death that, in addition to three physicians who were in attendati.., ,WO clergymen were summoned to my bed- side. At that tins mv wife's attention was called to a remedy which claimed to be a cure for rheumatism and neuralgia. She procured a toatk; and applied the con- tents to my head. It was liko a drowniog matt catching at a straw, it looked like the last hope. Th, remedy acted like magic. It saved my life. I feel sure, ;es; family and my friends tech sure, that had I not iced it should Mow be dead, instead if alive and hearty and in perfect health, as you st.e me here. All other treatment bad entirely failed, anti, wonderful to relate, I have never had the slightest return since I was cured sonie three years ago. I re-entered my old position, and in giving you the foregoing facts, I can only repeat that St. Jacob's Oil—which is the remoly referrtel tie-saved my life. My case is no secret. My friends and neighbours know an about it. My cure was considered so marvellous that I have received over 1.000 visits and letters on tlie sub- ject. To all of theme I have simply stated the facts 251 have related them to you. A call was the!, luade upon Messrs. Iludden & chemist,. 339 Stanley-roast. Kirk- date, from whom Mrs. Buchanan procured the Oil ; Mr. Gift the manager, fully verified the statement which had been made to the reporter, and said that this was only axe of the many remarkable cares, ffected by St. Jacoln Oil which had conic under his personal notice.

EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 12, 1889.

The County Council elections for Lancashire— that is where there are contests—are fixed for Tuesday next, and there is every evidence that there will be struggles on political lines in many of the divisions. It is noteworthy that, with the exception of Southport, there will he no contests in any of the Lancashire borough divisions. It would seen, that the smaller boronghs, which form part of Lancashire County Outwit. have felt that their interest could be best served by selecting representatives irrespective of politica. This view has largely obtained in Warrington ; hence the : proceeding of the Town COMIViI, a few weeks ago, I in naminii. gentlemen who would soitably repre- sent the borough. The proposed representatives I were not, le•wever, entirely to the taste of the two political panic;. The Conservatives were bent, as it transpired, inset nominating Mr. JOHN WHITE, J.P., whfle iiiii ny Liberals took exception to Councillor F. Moos, J.P., on the ground that he was a Liberal Unionist. There WAS no difficulty 1 with regard to C.llleillor FRANK A. ROBERTA, the Liberal candidate pure and simple; he was alike wholly acceptable to his party set to the Town Council. When the nominations came Sc, be pet in, on Monday, it was found that Mr. WHITE.: %MS I the only pensm nominated for the Southern Division; while in the North East Division I there were three candidates—Councillor Moses I Mr. II THORNTON and Councillor .1. If. FLEMINi: ..oservatives, looking upon the nomination • . •:. • P. a Fixer:in, who is a pneninent b• • ••• attack npon the seat proposed to be o' • • M r. MONKS, 1,10111i11111.A Coencill• I .1• . • • .• t the last moment, for North-West '1 • •I•position to • •coincillor F. A. in two divisions seemed • • • • • was avected by the with- ..•,•l:•y, of Mr. THORNTON, COM-- - and Councillor Jottay. Mr. ! .idinitted, when he was appealed , to to withdraw, that he had no desire to enter

the lists against either Mr. Etaluta; or Mr. MONKS, UO he had a high opinion of both ' gentlemen. With regard to Mr. Ftemmo it is due to him to say that Ins nomination was less owing to any action on his own part than to a desire oil the part of certain Liberals, who feel strongly on the . Rule question, to make a protest against the selection of a Liberal Unionist. Having made the protest, they will doubtless be content with having put it on record—so to speak. It is a matter of course to say that, oink, the Local Uovernment Act, as it uow exists, no question bearing on Home little. as the term is commonly.lunderstood, can possibly arise. Apart front politics, there can be no doubt as to Mr. Musks's special qualifications for the aim of County Councillor, and there is every reason to believe that he will perform his duties ma manner highly creditable to himself and the dirt- Mon he represents. W e certainly pmfur Mr.MosKS to Mr. Jens WHITE, who is too much of a landlords' agent to be an entirely free agent. It is some- thong to his credit, however, that, unless we are misinformed, be stmds in a line with both Mr. Moses mid Mr. Ronsars in being in favour of : such an extension of the borough as would, if made, enable Warrington to take rank immediately as a Town County. Looking at the Warrington election from a political point of view, it is at least gratifying to see the largest of the three divisions represented by an out-and-out Liberal in ! the person of Mr. F. A. ROBERTS, the Chairman of the Liberal Executive. He has aptitude for the work he has undertaken ; he has tact, courtesy, and large business experieniv. Warring- ton, it is now determined, will be represented by a Liberal, a Liberal Unionist, and a Conservative —three gentlemen, who, we do not doubt, will work well together in forwarding the interests of the borough which sends them to the Lancashire County Council.

"Art is long and time is fleeting " says the poet somewhat despairingly, but all poets are artists, and if they do not always achieve the highest art—which consists in concealing act— they nevertheless try, however fleeting the I time. It is in this spirit that the study of art I ought to be pursued, and it is in this spirit, we are glad to say, that so much progress is being made ,in this country, notwithstanding the justly severe , things that are said about us. Mr. JOHN RTLANDS, at the Warrington School of Art on I Tuesday evening, referred, by way of example, to the good engravings which he found in such a periodical as "Cassell's Magazine " compared with the illustrations published some years ago. We have in these columns commented on the same fact. We have before us the latest volume of " Casselfs Magazine," and a volume issued close 'on twenty years ago ; and one is as to the other I as far as illustration goes—as cheese is to chalk. Messrs. Cassell have always pre- ' seated the best they could supply for the money ; the difference in the two volumes really marks the progress of art in book illustration. The standard is higher, which moans that competition is greater, and that students require to work harder ti get is the front rank. Somehow, in these slays of rushing trains, and electric communica- ' Bon, we are always Iming urged on—" for ever climbing up the climbing wave "—and the ordinary student may well be tempted to exclaim—" Alas! is there no repose? But the searcher after truth in the realm of art has this advantage over wane other students ; he finds the beautiful in seeking . the true, and realises to the fall what Shakes- peare meant when he said—" The labour we delight in physics pain." Touching another point, Mr. C. B. Aylward, in the admirable address which he delivered as art mister, rightly observed that to those who were preparing to become art teachers " The greatest qualification is sympathy and true enthusiasm with the students in their work." There can be no question that Mr. Aylward him- self possesses these quitliiications, and we do not doubt that, under his direction, the War- rington School of Art will preserve the high roputation which it has so long and honour- ably enjoyed. In this connection, it is satisfactory to see that use acknowledgment was made, on Tuesday, of the labours as art master of Mr. C. THOMPSON who did so much for the institution in the past. At present the school is in debt; there seems to have been a bungling Chancellor of the Exchequer who didn't quite understand how to prepare his budget ; fir we are told with regard to an anticipated income that "the gentleman who made the estimate had twice over entered a very considerable sum." Who the financier was we are unable to say; we certainly do not imagine it could have been Mr. W. OWEN, the present honor- ary secretary, for he is too wide-awake, and too careful as to details to make a mistake of such magnitude. However, the mistake is being remedied there has bean "retrenchment and reform ;" and that there will continue to be " peace " it is a matter of course for us to hope. Schools of art are amongst our noblest institutions, and they are entitled to all the encouragement and support which the public can give them.
" TOUCH AND GO:
An epidemic of the worst kind of crime seems to he spreading over the land,but it is best,perhaps, to say little or nothing about it, for excitement produces excitement like begets like.
'Truth" says The celebrated Barnum has retired finally :rum the show business, having amassed a fortune of ten million dollars." Well dune Barnum! It is is princely fortune for the prince of showmen.

Mr. Gladstone visited Pompeii on Tuesday, and witnessed the excavation of a house, many entices objects being brought to light. It was a Cockney tourist, was nt it ? who said of Pompeii that" it wan a very interesting place, but dreadfully out of repair."

Forms of nomination ought to ho simplified : it is an exception for an ordinary elector to fill one up correctly. The latest notable victim is Sir David Ratcliffe : he is disqualified from stand- ing as a County Council candidate bemuse some- one has blundered.

Lord Thurlow, Chairman of the Salt Union, and others of that ilk have sent cheques to the Winsford Free Library. The total received for the purchase of books is nearly £2OO. Oh, that somebody would "salt" every Free Library in a similar way.

John Mullin, an old offender, appeared before the Warrington magistrates on Monday, and was sent to gaol for a month with hard labour, for stealing twobags of coal. There are various ways of "getting" coal ; but it is a case of "Mullin' it when it becomes a caso for the constable.

The Manchester Chamber of Commerce has not yet gone bodily over to the Fair Traders. On the contrary it has responded to the " uncertain sound" on the subject by passing,on Monday last, a unanh i nous resolution n favour of Free Trade. That is as it should be Manchester merchants have a reputation to maintain as men of sense.

0 When the enterprising burglar is a-burgling," and when he works as part of a gang, commences operations at eight in the evening, and shoots people down who interfere with him—as has been the case at Muswell-hill, it is time to consider whether it would not be wise to arm our con- stables with something more than a truncheon.

Mr. E. Harrington, M.P., has had is peculiar indignity put 1111011 him at Tullamore gaol he has been seized by the warders and had his Inoustache out off. Mr. Balfour's policy in Ireland was des- cribed, in the House of Commons, as one of " petty malignity and calculated brutality.' The treatment of Mr. Harrington is a compound of both.

Liverpool is becoming a laughing-stock by its squabble over the purchase of the "Captive Andromache." Let the authorities either buy or I refuse to buy, and have done with it. It is child- ish to talk of suspending the Autumn Exhibition ; because of a difference of opinion as to the value of a pkture. Little Peddlington might do things in this way, but surely not Liverpool.

A young Daresbury farmer, named Thomas Hayes, seems to hity3 lost his life by walking into the canal, on Saturday night, during the fog. It is lamentable to note how many lives are lost in ! this way. Canals and rivers under such circum- stances should be given a wide berth. A person who believes he knows a road blindfolded, may find himself misled in a fog,and a false step may he his lash

The Electric Sugar Refining Company has : proved the sweetest thing in swindles that has been known for a long time. It is no use asking why people are so credulous. Fools and their !money are 800111 parted; and it is a stock rule in the lying line that if you will oily lie in a really big style you can find folk who will swallow all you ' say as if R all were Goapol. Tho Gospel accord- ing to Electric Sugar ! Bah !

,1 The terrible tornado whidi has wrought such hideous havoc in the Eastern States of America ! is suggestive of the littleness of man and the great- ness of the forces ,•f nature. Men are killed as if they were fleas, as Emerson remarked of the earth- quake of Lisbon ; sod Shelley says The veleannes are dint. And the stars reel and swim When the Whirlwinds my banners unfurl.

It is stated that the following letter has been received by the Moroi- of Newport, Isle of Wight, from Sir Henry Ponsonhy Dear Mr. Mayor, —The Queen commands me to let you know that she is goingto npp Ant Prince Henry of Battenberg Captain and Governor of the Isle of Wight, in place of Lord Evvia!ey." Time wags the world. Some are bone greet, s,,:ao achieve greatness, but our German re!ati.ms have greatness thrust upon them.

A medical shan't ,f Sktton mulled John Wm. Bate vas linol .422 szyul :1 15s. ti.,nsts, at Run- corn on Moirly, bv an unnrovac3 assault on a farmer's sou II 111 Wilkie :on, also living at Sutton. Bab, ph,t.lvd ; lie coil it was an old debt he 100 l paid. It seems he had nursed Isis wrath and kept it warm for three years. The assault was a brutal one, and it would have served Bate right if the fine—heavy as it was—had been heavier still.

General Booth, reporting to the Salvationists , the result of au interview with the Home Secretary as to giving aid to the outcasts of London, said "if that gent!, nem hail not been so pressed with business he (Gem:nil Booth) would have got at him about his soul.- This r,inark mused we an, told, loud laughter. But why Is it very laugh- able to suppose that Mr. Matthews should have a soul ? Or does the fun come in at the idea of any Secretary of State having a soul worth saving ?

Originality is an excellent thing—except in the I case of the person who displays his originality by going wrong. Mr. Doom', J.P., the Returning Officerin the Newton-in-Makerfield Division,is not as a rule given to startling departures from the established order of things; he is not built that way"; and it seems a pity, when he did make up his mind to take a new coarse, that he did not, at 11 the same thee, see to it that it MO not a wrong I emir,. Mr. Gooca's originality broke out on I Monday, nod it took the form of ruling, when the nominations were handed in, that one nomination only would be officially accepted, and, further, that the Press should not be allowed to copy the nominations. All this was startling enough; but, unfortunately for Mr. GoocH, it raised the question so in, whether what he woo doing was" the thing from a legal point of view. The public thooght not, and the agents for the respective candidates tin eight not. And the agents reasoned with Mr. Gooco on the sub- ject, on Tuesday, when he acid. they and others attended at the Newton Town Hall to receive objections, if any, to the nominations. It was brought home to the Returning 011iecr, that, as the time had passed when any person could with- draw a nomination paper, it was not oven for the Returning Officer to select one and set the others mid:. It was f tether pinted out that the Queen's Bench might possibly be called ;omit to determine the validity of a nomination paper, and what if it should be found that the 0110 Mr. Gown had set aside as good should prove to be bad Was it to be assumed that the other nomination papers were not available ? Mr. Gown with plainly told that it would net be safe to leave some of the nomination papers unpublished ; and by this time, it would appear, that Mr. (loam had come to see the error of his The "Daily News " has done a good stroke hi ways, for he " caml in,- mut intimati,tl that " seearing aeoashae‘i essay._ they are peeseeted would accept all the nominations under the mr- , 10auer5-011 country aspects and country life.

It is rumoured that Mr. Gosehon, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, is about to replace the light gold coinage in circulation, at at cost probably of over half a million of money. This would he a boon, especially to bankers, and it is said that he has come to an understanding with the chief of them according to which, "if they helped him to complete his conversion of Three per Cent. Con- sols, this proposed rehabilitation of the gold coin- age will be their reward.- This may be a very clever stroke, but it looks very like a bribe.

: The current issue of " The Liberator " contains questions and answers relating to Nonconformity in a catechism "for the use of families and parochial schools prepared by the Rev. F. A. Ham. Here are two specimenic—" (Q) Is dissent a great sin ? (A) Yes ! it is in direct opposition to our duty towards God. (Q) Is It wicked to enter a Dissenting Meeting House ? A) Most assuredly" We should like to see the Rev. F. A. Once. There is something wrong with him. He ought to be medically examinol : there is either a soft place in his head or a hard place, in his heart. Alexander Wallace Ho ,gg is a wealthy merchant of Glasgow,who has been engaged in relining sugar and courting Miss Annie H. Mafarlane. As ought be expected he was sweetness itself—for a time. and in the heat of his refining 1018111088 he inven- ted a new sugar-emited tem ; lie wrote 3 letter from Manchester and zuldrcesed it to" Sandie's own dear Ritggitmluggie." There now: after that " lovey-ihivey is played out. "Sandie" seems to have collapsed after his great stroke; he couldn't keep it up,and now he is being sued, or pursued,for damages, awl damages, heavy damages, lie is likely to have to pay.

div.head: SHOCKING IICRDER OF A SWEETHEART.
div.p: SHOCKING IICRDER OF A SWEET- HEART.

The shrieking murder of a young woman was brought to light on Tuesday, at Otehilming, Surrey. It appears , that on Monday evening, an artist, named Jenkins, enticed his sweetheart, Emily Joy, a girl of nineteen, into his studio, which is situatial in a gotten, almost in the centre of the town. Ile there outraged her, and i then stratigkel her, and made oft, locking up the plitee. (1.1 I...testi:ly, he walked into the " Punclibowl• Inn. , about ten ntigntes distance, and confessed the crime The landlord at once took him to Onildford, and handed I ! hint over tn the police, to whom he made a staternind. Two constables were sent over to Godalming, and found , the body as described by the prisoner, the face being a horrible sight, a handkerchief being stuffed into Crh mouth, and a boa tied tightly round her neck. Prisoner was brought Wore one of the county magistrstes on Tuesday evening, and suffieient evidence having been given he was remanded until Saturday. Some blood has been found on the prisoner's shirt SieelreA and the Lout of WI shirt, which hg gays came from a bite which the girl inflicted on his finger. The prisoner also coolly states that Ile proved for the girl after he had murdered her. No motive has been assigned for the deed, but it is thought that the prisoner must have had his mind turned by reading the accounts of the Whitechapel tragedies, which he tried to imitate. On Thursday the coroner for Wed Surrey opened an inquest on the body of Emily Joy, at the Three Crowns Hotel, near Goialming. The first witness was Mary Ann Joy, mother of the deceased, wits said she last saw her da!ighter alive on Monday evening, when she and the pnomer went for a walk. Next day she received a letter feint Jenkins stating that the deceased and lie had decided never to part, and that they had gone for ever. He also asked that they might be buried together. Con- tinuing, witness said that, finding her daughter did not return, she went to the studio at one in the morning, but band all quiet there.—Police-constable Steel then th-Wriiloll the finding of the body.—Mr. Sallis, landlord of the Punch Bowl Inn, near Ilindhead, related the prisoner's confession made to him on Tuesday morning, andsaid he took him to Guildford Police Station.—Dr. Newman gave it as his opinion that the deceased had been outraged and then suffocated, and Deputy Chief Constable Barker having read Jenkins confession, the jury without a momenta hesitation returned a verdict of wilful murder against the prisoner, who was committed for trial gm the coroner's warrant,

div.head: LECTURE BY MR.- THOMAS MORRIR,
div.p: LECTURE BY MR.- THOMAS MORRIR,

At the weekly Meeting of tli2 tjtilin Mutual Im- provement Society held In the Drill Hall, Lymm, on Monday evening, under the presidency of 11r. Hy. Tetlow, Mr. Thomas Morrie, F. 0.5., of Warrington, gave an interesting lecture entitled "A story Of Two Stones and how they came to form part of the bread we eat." Mr. Morris, in the enure, of his lecture. remarked that the possibility of utiliring as a fertilizer tho material known no" Basic slag," " Basic cinder," "Meal," or by the more appropriate term of "Thomas phosphate pow- der," was seen at an early period of the basic steel pro- cess, although its .tual Introduction Inc such use only occurred some five or six years ago. It was ',maimed as a bye-product in the so-called Thomas and Ofichrist pro' I VW far dephosplmrizing in., a process by which molten pig iron was converted into a metal termed mild steel, but which was difficult to class either as iron or steel, since it pome.ed the virtues and vices of both. Such were the wonderful changes of nature going on around them that it was quite within the 11 possibilities" for them to be eating bread at Christmas which held some of the components of the ores and limestoneu of the species before them. The tors consisted of the most recently formed iron- stones that were considered worth alining and smelting; indeed, as a class, the ores of that formation yielded so low a percentage of iron that they were neglected when situated at a distance fronts any known range of coal fields. The expense in getting was very small indeed, the ore being simply shovelled into the truck from the side of the mountain. In the raw state the ores were passed into a calcining kiln, where at a temperature something below their melting point the carbonic acid , gas and other volatile gases were driven off, and the iron was brought front the condition of carbonate of iron . to that of the peroxide. That operation completed, the ! calcined or burnt ore, together with proper proportions! of coal or coke and lime, were put in the smelting fur- nace at the top, and in thecourse of 48 or 80 hours the molten metal which had been extracted from the iron- stones at an exceedingly high temperature was , tapped out at the bottom of the hearth of the for- flee, and ran down the channel and into moulds of sand that had been roughly prepared to receive it. Basic slag as it left the converting vesuil looked more fit to replace mate:Warn for road making than it did for put- tins on land to assist grass to grow, neithr would it Inc of any more nec there than were the pebblx tor small boulders that were exposed to view in some fields at every storm of rain, if it did not undergo a severe amount of crushing and grinding. At first bash, steel makers were not very succossful in their experiments with the reduction machinery used to produce the finely ground slag fertilizer, and the coarse qualitieo sent ant led to the farmers becoming prejudiced against the "iron" manure, but the difficulties were being fast got over, and an almost impalpable prodtmt was put on the , market, which would re-establish faith generally in the new phosphate. Wagner, in Darmstadt, had made a series of very elaborate experiments with different kinds ! of phosphatic manor., and the result was a great increase in yield in troth barley and wheat and othor crops (Applause.> Interesting Spirta were given is support of that statement. lie belit.ved, however, that samples of a scatted " Thomas Th.phate " had been sold u.s manure which had not contained a trsee of phosphoric acid. An experiment of Wagner's showed that theyield of grass in lbe. per acre was aa follows i—Cnmanured, wet moor land, 2,287 ; sandy water meadow, 1,559; meadow land ' with sand subsoil, 1,997; mattered with 535 lbs. of Thomas powder—moor land, 3,137; water meadow, 1,780 ; sand subsoil, 1,331. These figures showed that in the case of meadow land with sand sub.il the tables were turned against the powder,Onts denio.trating the rneed of agriculturists learning chemistry applicable ltivation. div.head: MELANCHOLY DEATH OF A DARESRY FARMER.
div.p: MELANCHOLY DEATH OF A DARES- RY FARMER.

On Tuesday afternoon Mr. J. E. IrVordey, county I coroner, held an inquiry, at the Ring o' Bells, Dares- bury, respecting the death of Mr. Thomas Lees, a farmer, lately residing with his mother at the Dairy Farm, Newton-by-Daresbury, whose body was dis- covered in the Bridgewater canal at Daresbury, on Sunday morning.-- Herbert Lees, Dairy Farm. Newton-by-Daresbury, identified the body as that of his brother, Thomas Lees, who was 0.1 years of ' age, and was a farmer. Witness last saw lihn alive on Saturday morning. Ile was then in his usual health, but bad Wen up late the night before attending a shoot- , log party. Dmeased was rather short-sighted.— Herbert Mayes, a fanners sm. Daresbury, stated that lin Saturday evening he W. on his way to Moore in company with his cousin when be met Thomas Lees , coming acres the fields fr. Moore to Daresburv. ' was about 200 yards on the lianebury side of the 'Bridge- water Canal. Ile askel witness to come back to Dares- bury but he refused, and instead asked LPN; to go on ; with him to Moore and they would return together. , Lees declined, and went oin towards Daresbury, witness I. continuing in the direction 44 Moore. It was a foggy night—it'. Thomas Jaekson spoke to having dragged the Bridgewater Canal at Daresbury on Sunday and racovered Ire,, the water the body of the deceased. It , was lying of, mt 50 yards from the Moorfield Bridge. He had examined the laxly, but found no marks of viie Ilence upon it. WARRINGTON CO-OTERATIVE SOCIETY.
NEW BUILDINGS.

For some time past the building of handsome strati ore has been in progress in Winwick-st., to I meet the requirementßof the extensive trade carried on by the Warrington Co-operative Society. In that I part of the town the nietubers of the society are very numerou., and the new huilding will prove a convenience to them, while it will to some extent relieve the press at the Sankey-st. establishment, which, although it it an extensive one, has of late years had its resources taxed to the utmost to meet the trade transacted there. At the Win- wick-st. establishment business will be carried on in the seine way as inn, Sankeywt. It is anticipated that tho work of building will be completed in March, and some time will afterwards be taken up by thin fitting of fixtures. Ise., before the establishment can be opened to ! the public. It is roughly estimated that the building will cost about £4,000, and it is expected that shout another £l,OOO may be requited for fittings and various incidental expenses. A pruninent feature lithe provision of a large roots intendivl for the holding of public meetings. Ti,,- Cseoperative Hall in Sankey-nt. will hold about 600 persons, but the new one in Winwickwt., is being constructed a little larger, and will hold still more. Mr. W. Owen is the architect, and Alossrs. Gibson & Sun are the builders.

-1:In ream OF A BAAANICS Situp—John Banner, Edpworth.street, sued Thomas Wakefield and his wife, of 328 Knutsford-road, for Eft 10s., the balance owing for fixtures of a barber's shim at Latchford sold to defendant by plaintiff. Mr. A. Brown who appeared fur the plaintiff said the plaintiff ...wiled the shop 328 Knutsford-road, which was fitted up as a barbers slop, and, after being inspected by the defendants, was sold to them Oa the 26th October. It was then agreed that a mot of 103. should It, paid to plaintiff for imme- diate possession and the fixtures,and a list of the articles to be handed over for that sum was given to the defendants. On the day that this was given, Mrs. ' Wakefield paid 190. on acemnit ; and a few days after- wards • further sum of LS 10s. lb, called evidence in support of this statement. Mr. Perey Davies, solicitor, for the defence contended that the articles sold were not worth the money paid. II Honour reminded Mr. Davies that as there was a specific contract the question of the value of the artickis could not be considered, and he should therefore, give judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed.

It appeared from evidence pro- duced by the plaintiff that he delivered 10s. to defendant whir acted as shareholder in the match, which took place on the 26th December. There was a dispute about the result and he instructed llill nut topay the money.—The defendant contended that he was one of the julges in the match and considering it fairly won he paid the moues' away. THE BRIDGE-STREET IMPROVEMENT, WARRINGTON.

Now that the Bridge-st. improvement is in a fair way to completion by the erection of business premises on most of the still vacant land it may not be out of place to give a brief sketch of its history and financial aspect. The widening of Badge-et. and particularly its lower pa ne, had been regarded as highly desirable, and, indeed, as fast becoming an absolute necessity, long before the work was filially undertaken by the Town Council. So for back as 1873 a provisional . order was obtained by the Corporation to widen the lower part of the street, and the same order empowered them to make an improvement in Scotland-road. Unfortunately, the improving of Scotland-road absorbed nearly the whole of the now that had been estimated us sufficient for both undertakings, and consequently the Bridge-at. im- provement bad to be left over.

div.head: IMPURE TILE TOWN
div.p: IMPURE TILE TOWN

The TOwli Council again took definite action in ! 1883, under the mayoralty of Alderman (at that time Councillor)Crosfield. Atthe September meetingof the Town Council, in 1853, the Street improvement and Lighting Committee brought forward a recommend- ation that it was desirable that Bridge-st., from Friars-gate to Bridge-foot, should be widened; and, further, that application should be made to the Local Government Board for a provisional order for carrying out such widening. There were no direct objections to these proposals, though Coun- cillor F. Monks argued that before going to the length suggested the Council ought to have an estimate or the cost. That, he considered, was only the beginning of a series of improvements, which, once begun, be could not see where they were to stop. An estimate in writing would, be pointed out, enable them in future years, when they found that the cost had been heavier than they then anticipated, to see who was to blame for misleading them. The Motor did not see any objection. to Councillor Monliti demand, and the latter was promised all that " it was advisable to give" in the way of estimates. At the meeting of the Council on October :31) of the same year, the Street Improvement Committee recommended that , the street between Friar's-gate and the corner of Mr. Marsh's shop, be widened to fifty feet, and they estimated the gross cost of acquiring the necessary property, together with all expenaes and the forming of the street, at ..ti:31,000, leaving about 6,1.15 yards of surplus land for re-sale. It was explained that every latitude had been allowed in this estimate so that it was not likely to be exceeded. Councillor Monks etniplained of the unbusinesslike way in which this business was being carried through, and he moved that the pro- posal of the Committee with regard to Bridge-st. be , not confirmed. This motion was seconded by Alderman Davies, but mover and seconder were the only two who supported it when it came to a , division.

div.head: GOVERNMENT INQUIRY.
div.p: GOVERNMENT INQUIRY.

The next stage was the holding of an inquiry by a Local Goveniment Board inspector at which a variety of evidence was adduced as to the desira- bility of the improvement. It was mentioned that ; the width of the existing foot pat h, in the narrowest part, was only :2ft. 11M., and of the carriage way 13ft. 11 in. The buildings that were to be pulled down were condemned by Alderman Burgess, the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, and Dr. Doman, the medical officer, as insanitary and the centre af disease.

Most of what was laid before the Inspector was strongly in favour of the improvement, but • the other side was not altogether unheard. Alder-1 , man Davies, who was not able to be present personally, sent a letter in which there was an objection and a prophecy. Ile wrote: I give ,my objection to proceeding with the scheme, and prophecy if carried out it will over-charge our ratepayers very heavily. I fear it will cost more • than treble the estimate stated by the en-Mayor." ' The tenanta of the doomed rhops were also repre- sented and put in a plea for delay, but this objec- tion was met by Town Clerk who pointed out that the Corporation would have three years in which to do the work. Ile added that." Its had no doubt they would find plenty of people willing to build shops as soon as the land was vacant."

NEW CATHOLIC SCHOOL AT WESTON. On Tuesday evening, at West., a new Catholic school, dedicated to St. John the Baptist, was for- mally opened by Dr. Mangan, of Runcorn. The building will meet, necessity that has long been experienced by the Catholic population of the township, and the Rev. Dr. blastaltli. the pastor to be congratulated upon the success of his efforts and those associated with him. Substantially built of brick, from the designs of Mr. Ilan, the sellool in capable of accommodating about 250 persons. It is well lighted, well ventilated, and is generally well fitted up for the purpose or teaching the young accenting to the requirements of the Education Department. The contractor was Thomas Kirkham, and the cost of the structure was about £4lO. At the opening ceremony there were present the Rev. lir. 05tstakli, Dr. Xlaturan, Mr. and Mrs. Borg-se, Miss Quinn, the Misses Clark, Mr. and Mrs. Birchall, Mr. E. Aaron, Mr. Dugmore, Mr. P. div.head: tetterg to the Obitor.
div.p: tetterg to the Obitor.
CORPORATION OFFICIALS AND ELECTIONS.

Sir—Have those who moved for and obtained a return of the names ansi salaries of the Corporation officials who acted as presiding officers and poll clerks at the last municipal elections Inst heart before they have carried their business half through ? I see that the return was presented to the Town Council on Tnesday, but nothing morecould be done because Councillor F. A. Roberts, who moved for it, was not present. I can assure you, sir, that there will boa grerlk deal of dissatisfaction if the thing is carried no further, but allowed to drop where it is. The return shows ono thing very clearly, ,uel that is that Corporation officials are, on the whole, very well paid for the work they do, to my nothing of whak they don't do, when they get a few eaten guineas at election times for leaving their own work undone and doing that which somebody else could do as well. Cane Corpora- tion official take a holiday anytime he likes ? It seems very much like it—Yours .1,11
Warrington, J. 10th, 1889. [Councillor F. A. Roberts, whomoved for the return, was, we believe, alwent from the Council Meeting, on Tues- day, through illness.—En. Es.]
WHO IS mn, GERALD W..RAWLEVS P "

Mr.—Some of my Newton friends have lately asked me the question—who is Mr. Rawlins, the candidate for the Newton and flaydock District County Council ? For the information of all whom it may concern. I beg to say that I have known the firm and their works upwards of 42 years. They were established in 1619 by Mr. Charles Edward Rawlins, late chairman of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce, end director of the Exchange Building Committee, one of the foremost supoorters of Cobden, Bright, Milner Gibson, George Wasn't Archibald Prentice, and others of t' Anti-Corn Law League fame," who crowned their great efforts in 1846 by removing the tax on corn, end enabling the people of Great Britain to obtain since then a cheap loaf. Mr. G. W. Rawlin.s and his brothers carry on the same works, near Rainfall Catholic Church, is smogs and ultramarine me. it If nily works of the kind in Great Brita tah.yrrterMlT the pleasure of going through their works and speaking to several of their workpeople—many of whom have worked there for 20 and even 55 years— and was told by them that if their conduct was right their situation is good for lifetime ; indeed all of them speak in the highest terms of Messrs. , Rawlins in promoting their social and moral welfare in ! every way they can. A proof of this is very observable at the works and the nice detached cottagm and gardens where their hands reside—a pattern to be imitiated, Mr. G. W. Rawlins, whom we hope to see returned el NI Member entire Connty Council, is, as may be seen, not unknown in this county. His family have long been identified with every movetnent cakulated to benefit the condition of the MaSSPS ; and it is to such as him, ant riot to men whose talents (if they have any) have been hidden under a bushel, ehat we must look to if our Councils are to bear good fruit men who are capable of grasping the many and various subjects that will come before them, with intelligent appreciation and sound mature judgmmt. Apologising for occupying no much of your valuable space,—l atn, Sir, yours truly, Newton-le-Willows, Jan., 1899
PRIESTLY INTOLERANCE.

div.head: W. URQUITART.
div.p: W. URQUITART.

Sir,—Not desiring to an advantage of the Vicar here, I drew his attention in November last to the source from whence came the Parish Magazine "Banner of Faith," before! hod seen the downright Popery it con- tained for that month, and asked him for an explana- tion, to which he has not vet replied. I see from the "English Churchman" of the 3rd inst. that it is pub- lished by the " lulburn Sisterhood," which is of the most advanced Romanizing type. What good can come from sash a quarter? It is impossible to hold Popery in one hand and the Bible in the other There has not been any Sunday school teachers' meet- ing here for over thirty months, and why? Was it because ones! the teachers asked him some questions on the Lord's Supper, and to whom he afterwards refused the ass of Church-st. schools to give an address on the subject ; also declined to take the chair at the Town flail when a competent lecturer on the matter was obtained. A Communicant's Union was formed in 1887, and instead of an addreas every three months, according to rule, only one has been held, at which a statement was wade that "The Lord's Supper was the greatest gift God had given us." When asked for Bible reference for such it is not forthcoming. I read some- thing different in John 3c 16e. The Bible Class for men, foundsd 13 months ago, la.stel a month; no discussion allowed; a similar rule at Runcorn. If a question is to be asked, it must he in writing, and it rests with the Vicar whether he replies on Sunday following. At one of thelargrnt churches (Emmanuel) in Liverpool there is a notice hoard with words on it—. Bible class for men from 2.45 to 3.45; discussion invited." Ile dismissed one of the most efficient Sunday sehool teachers, without ever consulting, the superintendents, or the teachers, or calling any meeting whatever in the subject, simply bvause the teacher spoke the truth too plainly for his ritual. _ _

Why did he refuse permixsion to the Rev. R. D. Munn) to hay i an evening communion in accordance with the Scriptures P Was Bishop Stubbs the lion in his way P The poor publican stood afar off, not in the holy place (an Ritualists say) yet he was justified. The Jewish Ceremonial laws were only :ill John ; after his titne the new Gospel covenant. worshipping, in spirit or truly; no priests (Eels. 4e.11-12vs.),altar or incense ;all these types having been abolished when Christ said, "it ishnished." As to the daily services, at times there ia only one per- am present exclusive of the curate, and bell ringer, when the Psalms are read over bv omitting every other verse. Is this reverence for the wisest of God? It is useless ask- biz the respective Vicars about these things ; they ' invariably give evasive replies. If this is the manner of lording it over the laity, the sooner the latter take the power into their hands the better. Witlinld thecash, the Parsons can always see you, or appeal if they want money yet too many of them want money and the power also; its too late in the day to be tolerated. 1 ROBERT FOULEEs. hodinin, Jan. 0, 1889.
THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
RUNCORN.

At No Man's Land the sixth copper dam is in construc- tion in the river, and a steam pile driving machine has been brought on the scene ready for using wooden piles in the sandy bed of the river. The operations have pro- gressed at arapid rate,and now about MO feet of the out- ride wall of the canal appears above the surface of the water. FATAL ACCIDENT AT LATCHFORD. An accident resulting in the death of a lad named Richard Phillips.l4 years of age, occurred on the LAtch- ford section of the Ship Cann!, between nine and ten , o'clock on Saturday morning. The deceased, who lived I with his parents at Hollins Green, had been engagril in , "• fatting "or greasing a number of wagons, and was getting from under one of them when the engine started. and his head was cut off and his right arm broken. Death was instantaneous. No one 'Witnessed the accident. An inquest tvasheld at theLatchford Hospital on Wednesday, to inquire into the rause of death. by Mr. H. C. Talon, county coroner, and after hearing the evidence a verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. STOCKTON HEATH TO TWEIVALL. The German navvy at work between Stockton Heath ' and Latchford is molting its way towards Lacthford Station,and the distance between the ends of the sections , , of the cutting is now very little over a half a mile. At the other end, although no steam navvies have been yet brought to the Latchford side of Cross-lane, the , Inman excavators haveMede a good break into thoground for a new cutting. Near the Hospital two American : exeavators are employed, one in levelling a bank in the , rutting, and others in widening the canal to the right. ! Further on towards Thelwall the men are busy at the formidable " spoil-banks " and other embankments. , The works are not, however, as active as usual, owing porliono to the uncertainty of the weather and the pro' "veto made at other points. FATAL ACCIDENT AT ECCLES. On Wednesday afternoon Mr. Coroner F. Price con- j ducted an ioqiriry at Barton, into the eircumstance.s , attending the death of Vincent John Solloway, aged 17 rears, who resided with-bin parents at 154, Ellesmere-A., Patricroft, and was employed as a "chain bus" on the Eccles section of the Ship Canal works. Ott Monday I afternoon, whilst deceased won riding on the loop chain of a laden wagon being drawn IT a horse, from the Jubilee steam navvy, in the Owen Park cutting te a , train of full ones, he fen, and the wheels of the wagon ' pasted over his head, and he was hilled instantly.—Mr. Colson. representing Mr. Walker, the contractor, said • notices were posted forbidding men and boys front riding on any portion ef the wagons except on the "mail" provided for the purpose, but unfortunateT ROMP of `he employes would not take the trouble to nod them. 71te Coroner said it was obvious that deceased was violating the rules by riding on the wagons, and no one could be held to blame. it was a pity workmen would not obey rules provided for their safety. The jury returned a venlict of " Accidental death." THE MISSION ROOMS. The" Chester Diocesan Calendar for 1039 states that during last year 13 places had been licensed for divine service. Six of these—those at Eistham, Ince, Stardom Point, Thelwail, Walton, and Frodsham—havo been opened for the use of the navvies employed entire Ship Canal works. THE MAKING OF NEW ROADS. Ala meeting of the Daresbury Highway Board, on , Thursday, a discuasion arose with regard to the making of new roads in consequence of the construction of the , Ship Canal. It was stated that the Canal Act stipulated that the roads should he thirty feet in width, and it appeared from the discussion that in the roads already commenced a footpath had been laid on each ride. the space thus occupied considerably lessening the width of the roadway proper. The Surveyor (Mr. Peerman) said that lie had not received notice that the making of roads would be commenced. It was ultimately resolved that the Clerk draw the attention of the Ship Canal COMpaIIV to the pietism of ire Act for the protection of the Board. r and ask that in future, before any new rn,ds are cum- I mencel, notice be given to the Surveyor, in order that I he might consult his committee on the matter.
SIR GILBERT GREENALL AND THE SliP CANAL. ARBITRATION AT MANCHESTER.

Mr. Betidell, M.P., sat on Wednesday, as arbitrator, at the Grand Hotel, Manchester, to assess the amount of compensation to be paid to Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Ml'., in respect to certain lands. amounting to about 41 acres, on his estate at Walton, near Warrington. The land is required for the purposes of the Manchester Ship Canal. Mr.. Bidder, Q.C., and Mr. Sutton appeared for Sir • Gilbert Greenall, and Mr. Pember, Q.C., represented ' the Company. Mr. Bidder, in opening the case, said Sir Gilbert Greenalrs estate comprised about 3,0(0) acres, and had been got together by various purchases extend- ing over along series of years. It Wfti in every way lan estate suitable to a gentleman of country tastes and of means adequate to indulge those tastes. The canal went through the estate and severed it in a , very serious manner. In this case beyond Vieques- tion on the value of land actually taken. there . would arise a question of damage and of com- pensation for injury to the rest of the estate by the severance and otherwise. A part of the estate was in close proximity to the town- ship of Warrington. The price of land in that particular locality was rapielly,rising on account of the demand for plots for residential purposes. The claimant, however, did not put down the whole of the land wanted as of building value. For one part he simply asked the price he gave to the Bridge- water Trustees—namely, £173 an acre. For the other portions of land, more fitted for residential purposes, he asked sums varying from Said to £lOO an acre. There was a farmstead completely destroyed by the canal, and the work entirely put • a stop to a large trade in moulding sands which . had been carried on with Warrington fora long Gine past. The canal had also dried up the water supply in that portion of the estate through which it ran. It might of course be said that the water supply would be returned with the completion of the canal, but that was hardly likely, seeing that the surface of the canal would be 301 t. below the land and consequently lower than the bottoin of the wells which nad been destroyed. Sir Gilbert's residence was 1,000 yards from the canal, and in that case no claim n•as made for residential damage. At the same time, Sir Gilbert WB9 a lover of sport and had preserved a great deal of game, and there would be a very considerable loss during tint: 2-19. king of the canal in everything wearing fur and feathers.

—Mr. John White (agent na the claimant) wan then called. He averaged the value of 41 acres at £250 an ' acre. To this amount he wiled the value of buildings actually taken, and, deducting chief rent, found the sum or £11,432 16s. as the value of the land. To that again he added osmpennation for injury likely to be sus- tained. The entire claim was £17,708 12,,

, Mr. Jacob Wilson Fair, survevor, of Haigh, near Wigan, said he had had an experience of thirty years in connection with the valuation of propertim. He was well acquainted with the district around Warring- ton, and had made a survey of Sir (filbert Greenaffs estate, and considered the probable influence on the property of the Ship Canal Works. In his opinion the canal works would have a serious effect on the rwidential property of the district. Not merely was residence made less desirable, but the means of commu- nication between one bank and the other of the canal were very inadequate. The swing, bridge would necessarily be a most uncertain means of communica- tion. The interference of the canal with agriculture would also be considerable. His valuation of the land, taking everything into consideration was £17,122. Mr. John Pierpoint, architect, of Warrington, esti- mated the value of the land and compensation for ' damage to the property at £16,640. SECOND DAY.

The arbitration was resumed on Thursday at the Grand Hotel, Manchester, before Mr. Handel, M.P. Mr. William Owen, architect, surveyor, and valuer, Warrington, said he was thoroughly acquainted with the district, being valuer to the Warrington Union Rural Sanitary Authority. ' He had known Walton for several years, and was well acquainted with the value of property in that locality. Ile knew the history of Sir Gilbert Greenall's estate. In his judgment the abstraction of the land for the purpose of the canal would seriously interfere with the residential ' value of the estate, and an injury would also be inflicted by severance The canal would affect the letting value a the hall and the sporting rights of the estate. Ile attached importance to the business to be carried on by the Canal Company. Ile had made a valuation. He had borne in mind the loss of frontage to the Mersey and Irwell Canal, and had taken that into consideration. It would no doubt, in Ida judgment, affect the agricultural value of the land. He estimated the net value of the land and buildings, with a percentage for compulsory sale, at £10,734. He added £2,721 for severance, and put the residential damage and damage to the estate generally at £3,200, making the total sum to be paid as , compensation £111,656. Mr. John Davies, Mollington, near Chester, surveyor and valuer, said he had made an independent valuation of the estate. He placed the amount for purchase and compensation at £10,521. Mr. TO. Burgess, bailiff to Sir. Gilbert &melon, and, nab-agent of the estate, gave evidence, and the case for the claimant w. closed. Mr. ('ember said that he would not address the arbi- trator, but would at ones proceed to call his witnesses, and would then contrast the evidence on both sides.

Mr. A. M. Dunlop, surveyor to the Ship Canal Com- pany, said he the value of the land on a compul- sory sale at £B,lBO lie thought £9,200 ample compel,' Nation from the Ship Canal Company. He liad put no depreciation whatever on the residence or on the estate, nor could he conceive that anybody could do such a thing when it was considered that the property was already severed by the bridge existing in connection with the Bridgwater Nevigatuon, now acquired by the
a

Canal Company. The bridge and the barge traffic were in existence before Sir Grilbert's house was erected, and the traffic that now went through there would continue to go through. There would be very little barge traffic on the canal, the traffic condsting principally of big ships. The company would continue to use the valuable property they bad acquired, and he could not see for the life of him where the depreciation to Sir Hilbert's MutiertY was, having regard to the fact that them existed there a navigable river and canal and two railways. Mr. Henry Linaker, surveyor, and valuer, Fmdsliam, said he was well ac, nainted with the value of land in the neighbourhood of Sir Gilbert fireenall's propeity. Ile had made a valuation of the land and buildings in dis- pute, and considered that the amount of eoinpensationto be paid by the Ship Canal Company should be £7,350. '"
Sutton, auctioneer and valuer (Mayor of Warrington), said he had made a valuation of the pro- perty, and placed the tr:ll.il amount to be paid at £B,IOE-.
THIRD T.
The arbitration wi.7;;;;;;W•at the Grand Hotel, Manchester, yesterday, when the evidence for the Ship 0p1p.,..ny was rrAumt.

Mr. JohtiCrl'iss, valuer, Manchester, estimated that the sum of £8,826 was due to Sir Gilbert Greenall, an amount including everything which he thought should he considered in valuing the land. In reply to Mr. Bidder, he said he had not the value of the moulding sand under the land when he made his valuation. Ha had allowed nothing with his valuation for the sporting rights, as he considered they were of no valus. Mr. John Simpson Patterson, valuer, Manchester, valuer for the Bridgewater Trusts..., the Ellesmere Trust, and the Mersey and Irwell Navigation Company, paid he had had o do with the buying and selling of I land in connection with those bodies., and he did not: consider there would he any nmidential damage to Sir Gilbert's estate. His total valuation of the land required in connection with the Ship Gana! was £9,228. In reply to Mr. gilder, witness did not think anything should be allowed for disturbance of sporting rights. Lle did not know that two covers had had to be given up in eon- .equenee of trespassing by navvies.—Mr. 1,9. Burgess, re-called, deposed to two covers having had to be given up because of the navvies trespassing in pursuit of game. —Mr. Simpson, in further cross-examination,said he was still of opinion that nothing ought to be allowed for interference with the sporting. Elias Horning, valuer, Manchester, said he estimated that Sir Gilbert Greenall ought to rewire £9933. •..,

, Mr. Pember said that wZrall the evidence he should I call. Ile had ether witnesses, bathe would not take up , more time by calling them. In that cane there were the ! goes ions of the value of the land, Ito severance, and residenttal value, all raised very much unusual. As to the value of the land he contended there had been great exaggeration on the part of the witnessss for the claimant. As to the question of severanoe, he strongly urged that the severance was very slight. FO slight, in lact,as to be scarcely worthy of the name. And as to the residential value, it was absolutely nomexistod. He would that deal with the value of the land which was the most important. The differ. once between the witmases on both sides was one of degree. By that he meant that the claim' atys witnesseu were a little too high in their valuation, while the company's witnesses were generally a little too low. Usually- a valuation between the two was taken, but that was a caso in which either the claimant or the company was wrong.and he took leave to say that hives the claimant who wan absolutely in the wrong. Mr. Bidder aid his witnesses lod stated what he could not help thinking was the origin of a mistake. They said in effect that Sir Gilbert Greenall had been slowly building up ale property by obtaining plots of land here and there, according asopportunity offered, until he; hod got 3.000 acres. Ile was a gentleman, whom he would describe ass otaalthy brewer, with a passion for the acquisition of land, an ambition for the possession of territory. Ile built for himself a large house and desired to collect a large estate. Of course, he could not follow Sir Gilbert Greenall all through the processm of acquiring the 3,000 acres of land, but they had one or two instanuis of the was in which he had gone to work, and the encumbrances he hats had to overcome. and how he had had to " pay through his nose." After instancing several prices paid for land by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr. Pember went on to =ay that all those ways of acquiring land involved a great deal of expense. Sir Gilbert hml been indulging- in the expen- sive luxury of getting together an estate, and the Ship Canal Company were not going to pay for that indul- gence. They intot only pay the real valise of the land, and Sir Gilbert Greenall was not entitled to say that because be gave too much, the company must also pay too mural. Yet that Was the position taken up by the claitnant. He contended that the land in question WAR not in the immediate neighbourhood of the town ; and was not particularly well situated for the develop- ment of a suburban neighbourhood. There v-as no real- way handy, and thee t wan no great convenience inroads, because, although there was one good road it was at a considerable distance front the land they wanted. Very little of the land required had a frontage loosen that one road. Another, thing was that the greater part of the land, he thought he roight say almost the whole of it, , had got a bail asuect, that was it fell to the Mersey, and got the wind from Widnes. A good aspect was that which : looked sotto over the country, and it was such land where building was going on. Sono of the land also was not fit to build upon. Mr. Pember proceeded to deal with the figures in the valuation of the various ! witnenses, contending that the figures given by the Ship ! Canal Co's. witnesses represented more truly the value of the land than did those of the claimant's witnesses. As regarded the claim for severance, one cause was the extra railway embanklnent, and the second WAS the course of the canal itself. The first was practically nil, and as regarded the canal it was obvious that it affected the homesteads only. Ile thought there were only two or three which had lands on the other side, and Mr. White himself said that would come to very littlebecause he had already made a redistribution of the land. That tliffieulty had been got over already. In regard to the residential claim, he asked what residen- tial injury could anybody itnagineto have been sustained from steamers passing along the canal at a distance of about 1,000 yards. No one could conceive any residen- tial inconventenee to arise from steamers going at the rate of Sort miles an hour at suck a distance; and be did not think any nuisance could arise from the blowing of fog horns and whistles which might be necessary. rhere was no severance of private or pleasure grounds; it was all agricultural land. These were the only points ! to which Ile wished to draw attention, and no doubt they I had occurred to the Arbitrator himself. He had not the I slightest hositation in saying that be would be ...nab. I Miffs award. Mr. Bidder, in replying for the claimant, criticinol the observations of Mr. Ponder at considerable length. He contended that as a residential neighbourhood the property would be prejudiced by the proximity of the canal, and it was not likely that people would build in such a position, where smoke from the funnels of the great steamers could be carried the ugh. The residents would have to put up with many inconveniences from the enormous traffic which Mr. Pemba- Woo SO fond of saying would he conducted on the canal. Ile had not attempted to put the case in an exaggerated forte, and he thought the Arbitrator would deal with the matter fairly, remembering that it was not a mere ques. tion of taking away so many acres of land, but also of interfering with that which, wisely or otherwise, Sir Gilbert (treenail had taken a pride in, namely, getting, together an estate in which Inc might take a pride, and which he hoped to enjoy. . . . . .
The Inquiry then terminated, and it wee understndl that the Arbitrator would make his award in due course.

FATAL ACCIDENT YESTERDAY.

. A -siT4ii-la—r -fatalityoccurred at Warrington yesterday, when John Broadhurst (63), a painter, who lived at 20 Napier-st., was accidently thrown from a cart to the ground and killed. The deceased bad not for some time been working at his trade, but bad earned a livelihood by going about with a home and cart, selling potatoes. At noon yester- day be was going along Coekliedge-laue, near to a shop kept by Benjamin Looker, at a part when the roadway is very narrow. At the corner of the ahop thereto a large stone, to protect the gable end of the building. Broadhurst was in his cart, driving past this stone, when one of the wheels caught against it, and he fell out of the vehicle, alighting on his bead. A cab was at once procured, and in it he was conveyed to the Infirmary, but he died before arriving there. The body of the deceased now lies at the Infirmary, awaiting an inquest.

SHOCKING SCALDING FATALITY AT WIDNES. i Yesterday afternoon, at the Widnes Accident Hospital, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of George Angus, who fell into a pan of caustic liquor at the works of Hall Bros. and Shaw, on the 2n4. inst. Mr. H. E. Rich- mond, WM. Inspector of factories, was present, and the proceedings were watched on behalf of the firm by Mr. R. Fogg.--Jolin Angus, chemical labourer, of William-st., Dutton, said the deceased was his brother, who was 36 years of age, and had resided at 10 Hartley-A He had twice seen the deceased in the hospital, but lie was not able to give any account of the accident.—Michael labourer, 44, Gerard-st., said the deceased wet his foreman. Ile saw him at a caustic pan containing hot caustic liquor., and then suddenly missed him. Ile heanl deceased shout, and saw him attempting to get suit nf the pan, but he lost his bold and fell back. Deceased now managed to jump out, and witness caught him in his arms. Deceased went into a tank of cold water.—Sfise Downie said the deceased was admitted to the Hospital on the 2nd Jan., the day he was injured. He was very badly scalded. He died on Tuesday morning. The deceased told her that be had been ill previous to the accident. He was on his way to tist the liquor, It-hers his foot slipped. and he atterapWl to right himself but failed owilig to his weak condition. Ile then fell into the pan.—John Robinson. analyst at the works, described the place where the aemliint was, and said the liquor was . heated to 180 degrees. The deceased was foreman , of the caustic department, and it was not part of his duty to test liquor in the wav be was doing. There was a ladder he could have used .for the purpose and he bad spoken to the deceased about the danger he incurred in the way he did. Every pre2aution was taken in the works to prevent accidents—The jury returned a verdict of accidental death, and added a rider that no bLvne was attached to the firm for the accident, but they hoped this would be a waming to be more careful in future. THE EARNINGS OF A ST. HELENS CLOG _ DANCER. _ .

Thomas Casson of Windle, a man of the street corner type. was brought before the Widnes magis- trates on Thursday to answer a charge of neglect- ing to maintam his wife and family. Mr. Stewart relieving officer, St. Helens, stated that on the 12th November the defendant,his wife and four children were turned out ol their house in consequence of non-payment of rent and he sent the wife and family to the woikhouse. The eldest son only remained there seven days, leaving to go to his grandmother, and the wife and throe children continued inmates of the abuse until the 29th0secin1or when they were dischargedat the woman's request. Their maintainence had cost the Guardians of the Usenet Union the sum of £5 lb. Bd. The pri- soner had followed the occupation of a chemical labourer, but he had not worked since August last. Ile was, how- ever, in tho habit of visiting public-houses and giving exhibitions of clog and step dancing and by this means he earned news than double the amount he would do in his ordinary employment. Ile had boasted that lie would never work to support his wife, and during the past six years his family had been several Mine on the point of starvation. The priiwner was sentenced to a inunth's hard labour.
MALICIOUS ASSAULT ON A YOUNG FARMER NEAR RUNCORN.

..... . A young man named John William Bate was summoned to Runeorn Petty Ses:sions,on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting Samuel John Within- ' son, a young man, son of a farmer of Aston Heath. The defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. A.Fletcher, who appeared to prosecute, stated that the Bench, after hearing the circumstances, would agree that the aswault was of a very aggravated character,and that the defend- ant ought to be severely punished for the offence he com- mitted. Between nix and half-past six o'clock on the evening of the 30th December, Wilkinson was going to his place of worsiiip at Sutton Bridge. Ai Sutton he met the defendant, who said, "Ratio. is that you; I will give you telling your—landlord about me," and without more ado he struck Wilkinson on the eye and belaboured him on the head with a stick. Wilkinson's face was bruised, and his ears and back of his head were seriously out. The defendant went away glorying in what he had done, and lie was evidently glorying in it that morning. The defendant was the son of a large farmer at Sutton ; he was a medical student and in train- ing fora veterinary suigeon. and of such a pasition that he ought to know better than to conduct himself in this way. The penalty to which he was liable was £s,and be (Mr. Fletcher) did not think there were any mitig,atingeir- cumstances which would induce the magistrates to make it less than that.—The complainant corroborated this statement, and said on Christmas Day he was driving his brother to Preston Brook Station. They SaIV thodefend• ant hunting with a dog, and his (complainant's) brother shouted, " I will let Colonel Talbot know of this."—The defendant, when asked if he had anything to say, said This is an old debt. Ile committed an assault on me in a similar manner at Sutton Weaver, and I hare had it in my mind for the last three or four years—Mr. Hotelier ! That makes it all the worse.—The defendant lam , obliged to you, but I feel as if I am satisfied now.— Major Harichurst (chairman), said it woos most unpro- voked assault,and the defendant was fined 40s, and costs £ll5B. ' On the re-aanimbling of the 'Court, the Chairman said the Botch feel to its fullest extent the great importance of their thity on this neertsion, and thave carefully con- sidered every point of evidence, and they are unanim- ously of opinion that no pr-Poo Pei,' case has been made out. Immediately the magisterial decision was given the unanimous approval of those present was expressed by a loud outburst of applause in court. It continued for a couple of minutes without any attempt to restrain it. Both advocates than thanked rhe bench in appro- priate terms for the consideration which they had given to the case.
